title: Your Weekend Eating Schedule May Affect Your Heart
paragraphs: Many people eat breakfast later than usual on the weekend, or have dinner at a different time. It may not seem important, but a new study from France suggests that changing your eating schedule on weekends may be bad for your heart, at least for men.

The study was published in the journal Communications Medicine in 2026. It used data from more than 100,000 adults in France who took part in a large, long-term study about food and health called NutriNet-Santé. Every six months, the participants recorded what they ate and when they ate it on three different days, including one weekend day. The researchers then followed them for about eight years.

The researchers looked at the difference between the timing of people's meals on weekdays and on weekends. They called this "eating jet lag." People were divided into three groups: those whose eating schedule stayed about the same, those who ate more than an hour earlier on weekends and those who ate more than an hour later.

The results showed that eating jet lag was linked to a higher risk of heart disease in men. For every extra hour of difference in meal times, men had about a 14% higher risk of heart and blood vessel disease. Men who ate earlier on weekends had the highest risk. Interestingly, the link was only seen among people who usually ate their first meal after about 8 a.m. In contrast, the researchers found no clear link among women.
Why might this happen? The researchers believe that changing meal times may disrupt the body's internal clock, which helps control many processes in the body.

However, the study had some limitations. It was observational, so it cannot prove that changing meal times causes heart disease. Also, most of the participants were women, and the researchers assumed that everyone's weekend was on Saturday and Sunday.
